zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent visual reading; the scan governs this transcription.

lines.note: Suwama nari continues the inlet-pattern entry from f460. The final vowel is a, not the draft i; the Portuguese means a shape or figure of this kind.
Laya completes the description of that kind of shape. This short row belongs to the preceding page's entry, not the following verb.
Suwari describes a thing being settled or fixed. The scan has capital S, not A; the principal parts are preserved in their abbreviated form.
After fixa, the meal-tray example has Ienuo, zen wo, and ſuuaru. The draft ſunani misread the repeated u and final ru. The Portuguese describes a table or tray being set before the speaker.
ſa completes mesa. Monji ga suwaru introduces the placing of written characters; Estar retains the draft's provisional short-s typography.
The character is set down in print or writing. Fune ga begins the next example with a boat as its subject.
Fune ga suwaru means a vessel grounding or running ashore. The two Portuguese verbs describe the same settled or immobilized condition.
Dô or kokoro no suwatta hito describes a person with a settled disposition. The printed circumflex in Dô is retained; the Portuguese homẽ is abbreviated.
The person is firm, constant, and settled. These traits explain the figurative application of suwaru rather than a literal seated posture.
Suwaya is identified as an interjection and referred to Suua on f460. The repeated u is worn but supports the full word; the grammatical label and Vide are italic.
Suuǒ is sappanwood, directly glossed Sapão. The caron is visible; this dye-material entry is distinct from the homonymous garment below.

runs.text: Hum vestido curto de mangas compri-

lines.note: The second Suuǒ is a short garment with long sleeves. Compri- continues compridas; the Japanese caron is retained without deriving it from the preceding homonym.

runs.text: das que ſe veſte por cima dos outros vestidos.

lines.note: Das completes compridas. The garment is worn over other clothes. Vestido in the preceding row and vestidos here retain their provisional st readings; veſte is not normalized to match them.

runs.text: Hum genero de mariſco, ou caſca

lines.note: Suuǒgai names a kind of shellfish or shell. The entry's geographic and shape description continues below, without establishing a precise modern species.

runs.text: que ſe acha nos prayas, que he como buzio.

lines.note: The shell is found on beaches and resembles a whelk-like shell. The worn vowel is provisionally read as o in nos prayas, retaining the aligned draft rather than silently normalizing it to expected nas; que replaces the OCR aue.
Suuoroxi describes falcons leaving the nest. The printed noun-like headword is preserved even though the Portuguese supplies an infinitival event description.
Suuǒzome is dyeing with sappanwood, linking the first Suuǒ entry to zome. The repeated u and caron are visible; the draft Sunǒzome mistook u for n.

runs.text: Hũa laya de vestido ſingelo de ſeda que

lines.note: Suxa is a single-layer silk garment. The adjective ſingelo and the material ſeda are retained, without replacing this historical garment name with a modern category.
The garment is worn on top of other clothing. This short continuation completes Suxa; the provisional st form in veste is not generalized to adjacent words.
Suxei is explained by the Japanese Cazuno foxi and Portuguese many stars. The worn vowel in Muitas is u, not the draft a; both Japanese expressions are roman.
Suxen is glossed many thousands. The short entry is complete on this physical row; no numerical value beyond the printed mil is supplied.
Suxi is fish prepared with rice and salt. Concertado is the printed historical word; the definition describes preservation and should not be silently recast as a modern sushi recipe.

runs.text: &c. pera durar, & ſe comer aßi crù.

lines.note: The preparation keeps the fish so it can be eaten in that state, raw. The ß in aßi and grave accent in crù are visible and retained.

runs.text: Salſa, ou couſa ſemelhante com que ſe

lines.note: Suxiuo is a sauce or similar accompaniment with which another food is eaten. The initial Salſa has a medial long s; the explanation continues onto the next row.
Come outra couſa completes the accompaniment definition. The row contains only Portuguese and remains italic, with its continuation indentation.
Suxo is many writings or scriptures. The first vowel in the headword is worn, but the surviving u-shaped strokes and the visible xo support the draft reading.
Suxǔ is equated with Cubimaqi, a small covering worn around the neck. Cubimaqi is a Japanese synonym after i, not a word embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: que cobrem os Bonzos o peſcoço atè baixo.

lines.note: The covering is worn by the Bonzos from the neck downward. The term Bonzos is retained as printed in the Portuguese, as is the grave accent in atè.

runs.text: Caſa onde ſe vende, ou faz vinagre.

lines.note: Suya is a house where vinegar is sold or made. The worn second letter has the remains of u rather than the draft a; the following row extends the name to its maker.
The same word also names a craftsperson who makes vinegar. Official replaces the OCR Officral: the damaged medial letters belong to the historical occupational noun, not an r.

runs.text: Certa feição de ferro de frecha.

lines.note: Suyaqi names a particular shape of arrow iron or arrowhead. The worn word is feição, shape, not the draft frição; the surviving e and the construction feição de support that reading.
Suye is an end or limit. The initial is S, not B, and the Portuguese reads termo rather than dermo. Suye fanjǒ begins the descendant-related expression completed below.
Suye fanjǒ is glossed the last or remotest descendants. The Portuguese completes the expression above; it is not the first sense of the following verb.

Suye is to put or set something down. Enlarged second-pass comparison with aßentar below resolves the looped double-s ligature as ß, not the draft ſt or two separate long-s types. The principal part yuru remains as printed.
Tacauo ſuyuru concerns taking or holding a falcon. Cou-ſa completes the opening definition, while le- continues the verb leuar on the following row.

The falcon is carried on the hand. Second-pass spacing comparison retains the draft's joined uaro, completing leuar o across the break, rather than inserting an uncertain internal space. Gibanuo ſuyuru starts the next example.
Gibanuo ſuyuru is to decide or settle something. Fanuo ſuyu- begins the signing example; the printed break in the Japanese verb is retained.

Ru completes ſuyuru, not the OCR rit. Ienuo ſuyuru concerns setting meal trays or tables. The damaged y has a surviving descender. The detached mark near u is compatible with the damaged long-s hook; a separate grave accent is not secure and is not supplied.
As meſas completes the tray-setting translation. Ginuo ſuyuru means establishing a camp; the gloss begins Aßentar and continues with arrayal below.
Arrayal completes the military example. Suuo ſuyuru is making vinegar, with the Portuguese vina-gre divided across rows; the two u letters in Suuo are retained.
Yaitôuo ſuyuru introduces applying points of heat or cautery, literally botões de fogo in the gloss. The circumflex on ô is visible; the example is not modernized.
Xeqiuo ſuyuru concerns establishing tolls or checkpoints. The X is crossed display-like roman type, not a different initial, and portagẽs retains its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: ou tomar portagens, ou tomar os paßos onde

lines.note: The Portuguese expands the checkpoint example: taking tolls or occupying passages where people travel. Paßos retains the ligature; the clause continues without a new example marker.

The clause concerns a place with much passing traffic. Enlarged second-pass inspection retains the aligned hi: the small vowel resembles a dotted i, and its worn left side does not justify a confident emendation to contextual hà. Comauo begins the horse example.
Comauo ſuyuru is making a horse stop. Yu- begins the bow example and remains a physical-line division, not a separate abbreviated headword.
Yu-mino fazuuo ſuyuru concerns trimming the bow tip. The narrow i after m is visible, restoring mino from the draft mno; fazuuo is kept as the printed joined form.
The bow tip completes the trimming gloss. Yumiuo ſuyuru begins another bow-working example; the terminal En has no secure hyphen, and continues in the next column.

runs.text: dereitar o arco dobrandoo hum pouco pera à

lines.note: En-dereitar spans the column boundary without a hyphen printed after En. The gloss describes straightening a bow by bending it slightly outward; dobrandoo and pera à are retained.
Parte de fora completes the instruction to bend the bow outward. This is the continuation of the final first-column example, not a new entry.

runs.text: Certa laya de abanos que tem as

lines.note: Suyefirogari is a kind of fan whose ends are open. The weak initial u is retained on the visible traces; abanos, fans, is clear in the Portuguese.

runs.text: pontas abertas, & ſerue nos autos, danças, &c.

lines.note: The fans are used in plays and dances. The printed singular ſerue is retained despite the plural abanos, and the ampersand precedes the abbreviation c.
Suyenarabe is to arrange several things. The headword and principal parts are roman, and the Portuguese begins the explanation of ordering them.
The objects are placed in order or evenly. This wholly Portuguese continuation completes the arranging sense without adding an example marker.
Suyetçumu fana is labelled P. and equated with Beni, rouge. The visible tç sequence is retained; Beni follows i, as a Japanese synonym rather than an embedded Portuguese term.

runs.text: Tina grande que ſerue pera ter agoa.

lines.note: Suyeuoqe is a large tub for holding water. The print has agoa and the joined headword; neither is normalized to modern orthography.

Suyeza, alternatively Batza, is the last or lowest seating position. Second-pass enlargement shows a t crosspiece and no i dot in Batza; the supplied NINJAL index independently agrees. The Japanese alternative remains roman, and derra- continues derradeiro.
The seat is the last place in the Zaxiqui. Zaxiqui occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is therefore a useful whole-word typeface-review target.
Suyezuye is illustrated by Suyezuyeno fito, people among the later descendants. Deſcẽ- carries a nasal abbreviation and a printed continuation mark.

runs.text: dentes derradeiros, ou poſtremos no parẽteſco,

lines.note: The descendants are last or remotest in kinship. The row continues the first Suyezuye example, with parẽteſco retaining its nasal abbreviation and long s.
The first explanation ends with generation. Suyezuye made begins a second example, extending the reference as far as the remotest descendants; the printed gèração accent is retained.
The second example means to the last descendants or latest generation. The local short s in descẽdentes is retained rather than made uniform with Deſcẽ- above.
Suzu is a small bell, glossed Caſcauel. The context is the bell sense of the Portuguese word, not a rattlesnake identification.
This homonymous Suzu is a needle-like fish, peixe agulha. The entry does not supply enough anatomical detail for a precise modern species assignment.

runs.text: Eſtanho, ou calaim. ¶ Item, bules, ou pi-

lines.note: A third Suzu means tin or calaim, and also vessels made from it. The entry continues with pi-cheis on the next row; the italic paragraph marker introduces the additional vessel sense.

runs.text: cheis de calaim que ſeruem de vinho.

lines.note: Pi-cheis are vessels of calaim used for wine. The metal name repeats the preceding row with a, not the draft u; the nasal-free spelling is preserved.
Suzucamo is a sea bird bearing this name. The printed entry supplies no fuller identification; the Japanese headword should not be expanded into an unsupported modern species name.
Suzucaqe is a short outer garment of Yamabuxi. The embedded Japanese name is italic with the surrounding gloss, rather than switching font for Y alone; the word continues as xi on the next row.

runs.text: xi, que ſe veſte por cima.

lines.note: Xi completes Yamabuxi, the name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, and appears italic here. The garment is worn on top; the comma belongs after the completed name.
Suzume is a sparrow, glossed Pardal. This compact entry occupies a complete row and is distinct from the following compound shellfish name.
Suzume gai is a kind of small clam. The headword is printed with a space, and the Portuguese ameijoas is retained without adding a modern species identification.
Suzumi means cooling oneself or going to a cool place. Its abbreviated parts u and unda remain roman; Refreſcarſe has two long-s occurrences in the printed gloss.
The person seeks cool air or a breeze. The grave accent in à viração is retained, along with the historical meteorological word viração.

runs.text: Lugar freſco, ou onde ſo toma

lines.note: Suzumidocoro is a cool place for taking the air. The tall d after mi replaces the OCR u; the Portuguese vowel in ſo is worn and retained provisionally rather than silently emended to expected ſe.
Àr and viração complete the description of a breezy place. The grave accent is printed over the initial vowel; the line remains a continuation of Suzumidocoro.
Suzumijo is referred to the preceding entry by Idem. The final jo is retained without adding a long-vowel mark from modern lexical expectations.

runs.text: Hum bichinho que cãta como grilo.

lines.note: Suzumuxi is a small insect that sings like a cricket. The nasal mark in cãta is clear; the gloss does not say that the creature is a different taxonomic group from crickets.
Suzuna is simply identified as an herb or plant. The sparse Portuguese definition is preserved rather than supplemented with a modern botanical name.
Suzuqi is a fish compared with robalo. The scan supports qi, not ki; the comparison is left as printed without narrowing it to a modern scientific species.
Suzuri is a Japanese ink vessel or inkstone, called Tinteiro de Iapão. The literal Portuguese label is retained, including Iapão with initial I.
Suzuribaco is the small box for the Japanese inkstone or ink vessel. The scan reads Caixinha with a, not the OCR Cuixinha; the Japanese compound remains a single word.

runs.text: Solda que ſe faz miſturada cõ eſtanho.

lines.note: Suzurǒ is solder made with tin. The tall letter in miſturada is long s, not l, and the scan separates cõ from eſtanho; the caron in the Japanese is clear.
Suzuxij describes something cool, such as wind or a place. The Japanese adjective ends in ij; the gloss retains vẽto and its visible nasal mark.
Suzuxiſa is the nominal derivative, coolness, printed as an indented subordinate form without a separate Portuguese gloss. The medial consonant is long s, not f.
Suzuxǔ is the adverbial form. Suzuxǔ mǒſu supplies a figurative speaking example; both carons and the long s in mǒſu are visible and retained.
The speaking example means speaking elegantly and politely. This completes Falar from the preceding row, extending the sense beyond literal physical coolness.
Suzuxime is transitive, to refresh or cool. Co- begins the following heart-related example; the scan shows an actual continuation mark after the Japanese fragment.
Co-corouo ſuzuximuru is to gladden the heart. The Portuguese is figurative; the physical split in Cocorouo is preserved rather than moved between rows.
Suzuxiro is identified only as an herb or plant. The short gloss is complete; no missing botanical explanation is inferred from the blank remainder of the row.
Suzzuqi is equated with Abura tçugui, an oil receptacle. The scan prints doubled zz in the headword and separates the Japanese synonym; teſ- continues teſto below.

runs.text: to que poem com azeite, & torcida dentro da

lines.note: The receptacle is placed with oil and a wick inside the lantern. The final article reads da, not the draft de; torcida is the historical wick noun in this context.
Lanterna completes the final S entry. The decorative flourish below is not an additional lexical line or the text s.; its erroneous OCR row is removed and the ornament is recorded separately.

zones.label: Closing ornament in column 2
zones.note: A centered, symmetrical ornament of paired brace-like and dot-like shapes follows the final S entry. It has no alphabetic text. The OCR's spurious body line c2-l045, s., has been removed; the visible ornament is preserved by this non-transcribed zone note.

zones.label: Printer's gathering signature
zones.note: The letterspaced signature Nnn stands below the ornament, separately from the catchword at the right edge.

zones.label: Bottom-right catchword
zones.note: The capital catchword ends with a clear double-stroke continuation mark, encoded as a hyphen like the other printed continuation marks.
